7255.title_en: The Story of Attracting Investors for a Startup, Part 1
7255.excerpt_en: Attracting investors for a startup, discussions with an Iranian accelerator, and the negotiation process and its stages, Part 1
7255.content_en:
Hello and greetings

I want to share my experiences in talking with various investors in several parts on the Mehrdad website. I hope these experiences can also help you.

I will try to write as concisely as possible and focus more on the useful points.

As usual, I have many projects and decided to list them. The number of projects was very large because I had been writing them for a long time and they kept increasing. So, I gathered the projects related to hardware and software and prepared 17 of them in a list for presentation.

I didn't want the project ideas to be revealed, and I knew some of them could be patented, so I presented them briefly and wrote explanations about each.

I tried to write the title and purpose of each project and explained its application and the potential revenue it could generate.

I prepared a PDF file and sent it to several people to get feedback. I looked for investors and accelerators, and through a Google search, I found a large number of accelerators.

From the websites of some of these accelerators, it was clear that they operate very superficially and weakly. Others didn't have a clear contact method. For example, one accelerator that had suddenly organized a large event had no clear contact method, which was surprising how poorly they operate. I think this website was just for show, or perhaps they had no intention of attracting projects through the internet.

I entered negotiations with an accelerator from Karaj. First, I had to enter information on their website. I spoke with the manager there, and after several conversations, we had good discussions, but in practice, this did not materialize.

They told me that according to the confidentiality agreement, I could present my project, and they have strong domestic and foreign investors, so I shouldn't worry about the amount of capital.

We agreed to set a time for an online platform meeting and consultation. A time was set, and the manager of that organization told me that specialists would be present in the meeting and that I should give a confidential presentation so that we could proceed according to the agreement for the next meeting.

In advance, I prepared a text and briefly wrote about one of my projects. I told myself to choose one of the projects with a good idea but test this accelerator with it, and if they responded well, I would present my other projects.

The online meeting started with a significant delay, as if one of the participants was on the way and didn't have a good internet connection.

The meeting started with me, the accelerator manager, and apparently two or three other listeners and specialists.

They asked me to explain myself and my background, which was strange to me because it wasn't related to the project. I explained anyway.

The specialist there also explained about himself, which I didn't think was necessary because the output, understanding, and actions of individuals are more important than their age and years of experience in a business.

I started my explanation. Contrary to what they had said about giving a confidential presentation and that the main meeting would be under a confidentiality agreement, they asked me to explain in more detail.

The meeting lasted about 45 minutes, and since I wanted to impress them, I gave many details and fully presented the idea.

The strangest thing was that they asked me to compare it with a strong sample that has entered the market, although some parts could be compared, and to tell them about the competitive advantages.

I mentioned about 10 competitive advantages, and it was strange that they kept asking for more competitive advantages.

More interestingly, there was another specialist there, and when the accelerator manager asked him if he had any questions, he said, "No, I'm writing." He meant my project, the competitive advantages, and other things.

The result of my thinking in a short time was easily in their hands, and since I had also worked on software analysis and the market, the project was very appealing to me.

I really don't understand, how many more advantages or options should one car have compared to another? That they emphasized competitive advantages so much. Of course, the project I presented was a super app in the business field, and there is still no complete sample like it.

In summary, the specialist insisted a lot and aggressively on competitive advantages, and I, surprised by the tone and manner of speaking, said so, and the meeting ended.

Seeing that they didn't have good intentions, I didn't expect a positive response because there was no confidentiality agreement, and it wasn't clear exactly who these people were that they could receive a design and solution so easily and have no legal commitment in exchange for the formula they received.

And the result for startup funding was not positive, and they didn't give reasons for rejection, and it didn't even occur to them that the confidentiality agreement and privacy had not been respected as per our conversations.

Based on my own experience, I don't expect everyone to give a positive response, and hearing more negative responses is more logical, but this type of experience was also interesting.

In my next writings, I will continue to share my experiences in raising capital for startups.

Thank you

7256.content_en:
With greetings and salutations

It has been a long time since Google has blocked its services for Iranians

That means even before the sanctions, we didn't have access to some of Google's services, and with the implementation of sanctions, these restrictions have become much more severe

I remember that even a long time ago, they wouldn't include Iran as a country in apps and famous websites like Google, Yahoo, Microsoft

Even though they had many users from Iran

In my opinion, this was a malicious policy that was from the very beginning intended for Iranians and Persian speakers in particular.

The same issue of the clash between Western and Eastern cultures that we see in movies and media is interesting; they have no other enmity with the East and only Iran matters to them. The Chinese have become so powerful that the West cannot consider any confrontation with them, or if it's an economic war like between Samsung and Apple, the playing field is clear.

But what is not clear to ordinary Iranian users and experts is their confusing policy with us.

They have a problem with the government but in practice, they have targeted the people, and most people suffer more.

For years, mobile developers have encountered problems in Google panels, and we use various methods to bypass sanctions, but they still identify and remove our applications or completely close the developer panel.

So why is Google important when there are Cafe Bazaar and other app markets for mobile applications?

Well, Cafe Bazaar has its own monopolistic policy and blocks certain apps while promoting others. What we see is that there is no fairness in their work, and if it weren't for Google's sanctions, Cafe Bazaar and others wouldn't even have been around to compete.

For the mobile app market, Cafe Bazaar has benefited the most from the sanctions by attracting many users and creating a monopoly market where many apps, after spending a lot of money, couldn't secure their position, like Sheypoor and …

Cafe Bazaar has a policy that for in-app payments, we must use Cafe Bazaar's own payment gateway, but in Google, even for us Iranians, we can define Iranian bank gateways and there is no Google in-app payment. ( play.google.com)

Compared to Cafe Bazaar, Google is a place where we can be free from this monopoly and have healthier competition. Separately, by receiving services like Google AdMob, we can earn in foreign currency (dollars) and even build global applications.

When the market is freer, there is healthier competition and higher revenue for apps that put in more effort or use more effective techniques in digital marketing.

Unfortunately, despite having influential Iranians at Google, I have never seen them try to advocate for the rights of experts in this field. They just boast about working at Google and take pride in being Iranian, which in my opinion is just to attract attention and build their personal brand.

One solution I found was to ask Iranians who are abroad to create accounts for us, and through a VPS, we can manage and publish our applications.

Of course, there are individuals who create accounts and sell them at high prices, for example, 8 to 12 million. Consider that the cost of creating an account is only 25 dollars, which is about 1 million tomans. But because of sanctions, we have to pay 12 times more to create another identity for ourselves and be able to present our business.

To create an account, you need to visit the address below and after entering the information, pay 25 dollars to activate your account.

https://play.google.com/console

Developer accounts, by connecting to google admob, can boost our business. Of course, for the Google AdMob part, you need to receive money through an intermediary, and that has its own separate story.

I will try to talk more about this in my next posts and discuss earning through Google AdMob more.

7258.title_en: Mehrdad { mehrdad }: History and Meaning of the Name Mehrdad
7258.excerpt_en: Here, we want to discuss the name Mehrdad and its history. Mehrdad is a Persian name that is very ancient and was used to name several kings during the Parthian era in Iran. The name Mehr is a very common name, and the month of Mehr is also named after it in Iran [...]
7258.content_en:
Here we want to talk about the name Mehrdad and the history of this name

src="/media/Coin_of_Mithradates_I_of_Parthia_Seleucia_mint.jpg"Silver coin of Mithridates I

The name Mehrdad is a very old Persian name that was also chosen for several kings during the Parthian period in Iran. The name Mehr is a very common name, and there is also a month named Mehr in Iran.

Other names that start with Mehr include the following names

Mehrshad- Mehran- Mehrab- Mehrad- Mehraneh- Mehrzad- Mehri- Mehrsa- Radmehr- Mehrazad- Shadmehr- Mehroush- Bozorgmehr- Mehrta- Zadmehr- Mehrdokht- Mehravrid- Mehrush- Mehrigan and others…

 

 

Persian Wikipedia

Mehrdad is one of the Iranian names for men. This name is one of the original Persian names that was used for the kings of Iran during the Arsacid period.

Mehrdad is derived from Middle Persian Mihrdat, meaning "given by Mehr." Mehr in turn is derived from Avestan Mithra, the Zoroastrian divinity of covenant. In modern Iran, the name Mehrdad is also used to refer to several historical figures known in Western literature as Mithridates, the Hellenized form of Mehrdad. This name consists of two parts: Mehr meaning sun and Dad meaning creator (creator of the sun); and it was the name of two of the greatest kings of Iran and the Arsacids. (Pronunciation: mehr dād) Gift of Mehr, created by Mehr; (in history) the name of three Arsacid kings was Mehrdad (Arsacid kings 6, 9, 13); Mehrdad was also the name of one of Astyages' appointees who Cyrus was entrusted to; and also the name of Khosrow Parviz's son. Also, in some old books, it has been used as the word for prophet.

 

 

The meaning of the name Mehrdad

Gift of the Sun

Origin of the name Mehrdad

Persian name

Dehkhoda's dictionary mentions the following for Mehrdad

Mehrdad I

Mehrdad I. [m d a v] (Akh) Arsacid VI. The sixth king of the Arsacid dynasty. He brought the Arsacid empire to its peak of power and defeated and captured Demetrius, the king of the Seleucids. He was the first king of the Arsacids to call himself King of Kings and reigned from 173 to 140 BC.

Mehrdad II

Mehrdad II. [m d du] (Akh) Arsacid IX. Titled the Great. The ninth king of the Arsacid dynasty and one of the most famous, who reigned from 124 to 76 BC. He defeated the Scythians, established trade relations with China, and in 92 BC made a friendship treaty with the Roman state and conquered Mesopotamia around 90 BC.

Mehrdad III

Mehrdad III. [m d s v] (Akh) Arsacid XII. The twelfth Arsacid king (56-55 BC). He killed his father, Phraates III, and went to extremes in cruelty and ruthlessness until they rebelled against him and brought his brother Orodes to the throne. See History of Iran by Mirza Mohammad Khan Qajar, p. 151.

Mehrdad IV

Mehrdad IV. [m d ch r] (Akh) King of Parthia, titled Philopator Philadelphus. He apparently reigned from 170 to 150 BC, during the period between the death of Phraates II and the end of the reign of Balash II in Iran, but no documents or writings from his time exist.

Mehrdad V

Mehrdad V. [m d p j] (Akh) King of Parthia, titled Euergetes, who apparently reigned from 150 to 121 BC and made peace with the Romans during his reign.

 

Mehrdad VI

Mehrdad VI. [m d sh sh] (Akh) Son of Mehrdad V and titled Eupator, known as the Great. He was born around 132 BC and reigned from 120 to 63 BC. There is no precise information about his youth and the beginning of his reign. Gradually, he gained control over Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, Bithynia, and all the southern and eastern parts of the Black Sea. His opposition to the kings of Bithynia led to his enmity with the Roman state, which caused Mehrdad to fight the Romans three times, and these wars are known in history as the Mithridatic Wars. In the first Mithridatic War, which lasted from 88 to 84 BC, Mehrdad initially achieved some victories until his general in Greece was defeated by the Roman general Sulla, and Mehrdad was forced to make peace and pay a large indemnity. The second Mithridatic War lasted from 83 to 81 BC. In this war, Mehrdad defeated the Roman army and attacked Pontus. In the third war (74-64 BC), Mehrdad occupied Bithynia and recaptured Pontus (68-67 BC). But he was defeated by the Roman general Pompey in 66 BC and fled to Crimea, where he eventually committed suicide. Mehrdad VI was one of the greatest commanders in history and the greatest enemy of Rome in all ages. See History of Iran by Mirza Mohammad Khan Qajar, pp. 147-149.

 

Laodice

Laodice. [u] (Akh) Daughter of Mehrdad II, king of Pontus, whom Antiochus III (the Great) married after making an alliance with Mehrdad. (221 BC) (Ancient Iran, vol. 3, p. 2080)

Mithridatium
Dehkhoda's Persian Dictionary

(m r) [ma'r.] (A.) an antidote elixir, the preparation of which is first attributed to Mithridates, king of Pontus from the Parthian dynasty; mithridatium.

 

Wikipedia says the following about Mehrdad

Mehrdad I (in Pahlavi: Mihrdāt), Arsacid V in the new count, known as Mehrdad the Great[1], was the King of Kings of Iran from 171 BC to 132 BC and the main architect of the Arsacid Empire. His conquests transformed the Arsacid state from a small kingdom into a world empire and one of the greatest powers of his time.[2] He was the first Arsacid king to adopt the title of the Achaemenid kings, King of Kings.

Name

Mehrdad means "given by Mehr." This name comes from the Old Persian Miθradāta. Its Pahlavi (Parthian) form was Mihrdāt, and the Greeks and Romans called it Mithridates.

The Old Persian form is Mithradāta, while in Modern Persian it is Mehrdad (Mehrdad).

Family and Accession

Mehrdad was the son of Friapati and the grandson of Arsaces I. He had several brothers, the eldest of whom, Phraates I, had ascended the throne in 176 BC after their father.

According to ancient custom, the king should choose one of his sons as his successor, but although the children of Phraates had priority over Mehrdad I in the line of succession, he broke the custom and chose his brother as his successor because of the abilities he had shown.[1][3]

Reign

After the death of Phraates I, Mehrdad ascended the throne in his place. In his first major military operation, he turned toward the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. The Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, which had been weakened by long wars with Sogdia and Indian states, was hardly defeated by the Arsacid king, and Mehrdad entered Bactria and annexed the region to his empire.[1]

After that, Mithridates turned his attention to the Seleucids. In 146 BCE, he attacked Media and captured Hamadan.[4] Following this, in 141 BCE, he entered Babylon and Mesopotamia, where he was officially crowned as King of Kings of Iran.[5] Coins from this period, minted in the city of Seleucia, have survived. After that, he went to Gorgan to defend the northern borders of the Parthian Empire. At the same time, Parthian generals conquered Persia and Elam in his name.

 

src="/media/Conquest_of_Mithridates_I.svg_-1024x531.png"Map of Mithridates I's rule Mithridates I's conquests

While the city of One Hundred Gates was chosen as the first capital of the Parthian Empire, Mithridates I also established royal residences in Seleucia, Ecbatana, Ctesiphon, and his newly founded city of Mithradatkert. Additionally, Mithradatkert was the location where a tomb was built for and maintained the Parthian kings.[6] On the other hand, Ecbatana became the summer residence of the Parthian royal family.[7] The city of Ctesiphon was not chosen as the capital until the reign of Gotarzes I,[8] but according to Brosius, it was used as a location for coronations and was a symbolic city of the Parthian rule.[9]

In 140 BCE, the Seleucids again attacked Mesopotamia. While Mithridates was busy fighting the Scythians in the east,[11] Demetrius II Seleucus conquered Mesopotamia. However, the Seleucids were soon defeated and driven out in the same year. Even Demetrius himself fell into the hands of the Parthians and was sent to Gorgan to Mithridates. He received the Seleucid king warmly and even gave his daughter, Rhodogune, in marriage to him.[12] Mithridates then punished the king of Elam for helping the Seleucids.[13][11] The Parthian King of Kings also allowed Vardfradad II, the frataraka of Persis, to have more autonomy in his domain. Mithridates died in 132 BCE and Phraates II succeeded him.

Coins and Imperial Ideology

From the early years of the second century BCE, the Parthians placed greater emphasis on their claim to be the successors of the Achaemenid Kings of Kings. They claimed that Arsaces, the first Parthian king, was a descendant of Artaxerxes II, the Achaemenid King of Kings.[14] The royal titles of the Achaemenids were also revived during the Parthian period, the most important of which was the title "King of Kings" (Shahanshah). Mithridates I was the first Parthian ruler to mint coins with this title, however, it took until the time of Mithridates II for this title to become the usual title of Parthian kings.[14][11] Also, the early Parthian kings depicted themselves on their coins wearing the Median tiara.[14]

src="/media/1200px-Xong-e_Ashdar_Parthian_relief-1024x768.jpg"Parthian Mithridates relief Parthian Mithridates relief in Khuzestan

The earliest coins of Mithridates I also show him wearing the Median tiara. However, as the power of this King of Kings grew, he was depicted on his newer coins with a royal diadem.[15][16] He also adopted some Hellenistic traditions, but unlike Greek rulers and early Parthians, he was depicted on his coins as a bearded man, which was a sign of his claim to be the successor of the ancient Iranian Kings of Kings.[16]

Mithridates I also had the title Philhellene (Friend of the Greeks) inscribed on his coins after conquering Mesopotamia to establish friendly relations with the Greeks whose lands he had recently conquered.[17] Another title he inscribed on his coins was "Arsaces" which later changed to "Arsaces King" and eventually became "Great King Arsaces".[16] Arsaces, the name of the first Parthian king, was the official name of all Parthian Kings of Kings until the fall of this dynasty.[1][18]

"Whose father is a god" was another title of Mithridates I. Phraates II, his successor, also had this title inscribed on his coins.[16]

Legacy

The most important achievement of Mithridates during his lifetime was transforming the Parthian kingdom from a local ruling power into a world empire.[11] He pursued this goal through his conquests in the west, aiming to reach the Mediterranean by dominating Syria and establishing Iranian hegemony over that region. However, this goal became a major conflict between Iran and Rome that lasted until the end of the Sassanian period and did not reach any definitive conclusion.[11] As Mithridates is considered the main architect of the Parthian Empire, some place him alongside Kings of Kings such as Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Achaemenid Empire

7265.content_en:
We want to discuss here what steps creating a robot might involve?

As you know, with the launch of the smart chatgpt robot, the market for building robots has heated up. We explain the steps of building a robot here, of course, we have used the chatgpt robot itself for help.

Starting a startup to build a robot can be a big and interesting project. To get started, you can use the following steps:

  1. Determine the goal: The first step to start a startup for building a robot is to determine the goal. You should know what your robot is built for and what services it will provide to its user family.

  2. Market research: After determining the goal, you should research the market and see if there are any similar robots with similar services in the market. If yes, you should know what advantages you have for your robot and how you can differentiate yourself from your competitors.

  3. Determine the team: After market research, you should determine what team you need. If you don't have the necessary skills to build the robot, you should seek help from experts. Selecting team members is one of the most important tasks.

  4. Design the robot: After determining the team, you should plan for your robot and define all the features, capabilities, and services.

  5. Develop the robot: After design, you should start developing the robot. This stage may include software development, testing, improvement, and code repair.

  6. Test the robot: After development is complete, you should test the robot with users and see if it works well. If you encounter problems, you should improve them.

  7. Launch and sales: After completing tests and review, you should release your robot for sale. You can sell your robot on online stores, specialized websites, or through social media channels.

    1. Manage the robot: After launch, you should define rules and procedures for good management of your robot. You should mention necessary updates and improvements for improving the robot's performance and user satisfaction.

    2. Improve and update the robot: You should regularly improve your robot and update it using new technologies.

    3. Check user satisfaction: You should regularly check user satisfaction with your robot and improve it based on their comments and requests.

    As you can see, creating a startup to build a robot is a time-consuming project and involves various stages and responsibilities.

src="/media/183391-1.jpg"Design and programming of a smart robot

For robot programming, you can use different programming languages such as Python, Java, C++, etc.

The main goal of robot programming is to create a computer program that can automatically respond to user requests without the need for human input.

The programming work starts as follows:

  1. Define the problem: First, you need to define the problem and determine the robot's goal.

  2. Define the algorithm: After defining the problem, define the algorithm to solve the problem.

  3. Write the code: After defining the algorithm, start writing the code for your robot. In this step, you need to define the necessary parameters and functions according to the chosen programming language.

  4. Execute the code: After writing the code, we run and test it on the dataset.

  5. Also, it is important to improve the program and prevent potential errors by using appropriate methods for updating, testing, error detection, etc.

    In addition, you should consider that the robot's responses should be appropriate, valid, and accurate. Therefore, you should prepare the program for users using appropriate methods.

    Finally, you should pay attention to the efficient development and improvement of the program and improve it using new advancements in the field.

7268.title_en: How Should Startup Team Building Be?
7268.excerpt_en: Startup team building requires selecting suitable individuals according to their roles and responsibilities, active coordination and communication, high motivation and commitment, and abundant capabilities.
7268.content_en:
Team building in startups is a vital and fundamental matter and is considered one of the key factors in the success of a young company. Below, some of the most important points to consider in startup team building are mentioned:

  1. Reviewing Strengths: Initially, the strengths and necessary skills for starting a young company must be carefully examined, and individuals with diverse expertise should be selected to form the team.

  2. Defining Roles and Responsibilities: The roles and responsibilities of each team member must be determined, and tasks should be allocated according to the expertise and capabilities of each individual.

  3. Coordination and Communication: Startup teams require active coordination and cooperation with each other to succeed, so communication and coordination among team members are extremely important.

  4. Collaboration Ability: In startup team building, attention should be paid to individuals who have the ability to collaborate and work in groups and have the capability to build a strong and effective team.

  5. Motivation and Commitment: Team members must have high motivation and commitment to be able to strive with focus and determination to achieve the company's goals.

  6. Shared Identity: A shared identity for the team should be defined that all team members follow and act upon.

  7. Individual Diversity: Teams consisting of individuals with different areas of expertise

src="/media/080921_The-Importance-Of-Branding-In-Businesses_2-how-to-create-a-great-brand-1024x536-1.jpg"What should startup team building be like?

Teams consisting of individuals with diverse expertise are of high importance for creating diverse and appealing products, so we must pay attention to the fact that individual diversity in the team is very important.

  1. Problem-Solving Ability: Startup teams must have the ability to solve problems to succeed and be able to address customer concerns with creative ideas.

  2. Transparency and Trustworthiness: Transparency and trustworthiness in dealing with colleagues, customers, and other stakeholders are important and should be considered in team building.

  3. Leadership: Strong and effective leadership in startup teams is of very high importance, and an individual with suitable and reliable leadership abilities should be chosen as the team leader.

  4. Adaptability to Change: In the world of startups, conditions and work environments are very dynamic and changeable, therefore startup teams must be able to adapt to changes and revise their own strategies.

    1. Creativity and Innovation: In the startup industry, creativity and innovation are of very high importance, so attention should be paid to individuals who have the ability to be creative and generate new ideas.

    In general, startup team building requires selecting suitable individuals according to their roles and responsibilities, active coordination and communication, high motivation and commitment, and abundant abilities.

Tolerance for pressure and stress, problem-solving ability, transparency and trustworthiness, leadership, adaptability to change, and creativity and innovation. Considering these points, actions can be taken for startup team building, such as introducing and interviewing new candidates, training and enhancing team skills, providing opportunities for synergy and collaboration, encouraging the sharing of ideas and suggestions, promoting problem-solving and offering innovative solutions, and focusing on improving the decision-making process and internal communication.

In addition, paying attention to organizational structure and work processes is also very important in startup team building. Startup teams should have a flexible and adaptable structure that can keep up with dynamic changes in the market and technology. Also, work processes should be designed in a way that uses less time and energy to complete tasks and focuses more on providing appealing and efficient products.

Finally, it should be noted that team building in startups is a continuous process that requires constant review and modification. Therefore, startup teams should pay attention to customer feedback, data analysis, and their past experiences to improve and enhance their performance.

src="/media/img-stories-hero-1024x539.png"Team building in a startup

To improve their team skills, they should seek growth and progress. Also, by holding periodic meetings to review team performance and plan for increasing productivity and improving team performance, team building can be taken to a higher level.

In general, to have an efficient organizational team in a startup, it is necessary to pay attention to matters such as selecting the right people, developing individual and team skills, designing flexible organizational structures and work processes, high communication, and paying attention to customer feedback. These factors will enable the startup team to offer higher quality and more appealing products and services and achieve success in the market.

 

Thank you Mehrdad

7281.content_en:
With greetings and respect

Room Topic: Why no matter how hard we try, nothing changes
Event Time: 10:30 PM to 2:00 AM on October 30, 2021
src="/media/Screenshot_۲۰۲۱۱۰۲۵-۲۳۴۹۰۷_Clubhouse-e1635247821757-247x300.jpg"Clubhouseکلاب هاوس
With the proposal of Mr. Hamed Hedayati and managed by Mehrdad, we held a room about change
Different people participated in the room and expressed their views, which sometimes became challenging discussions
Some people also shared memories about how change and transformation occur
Many people joined and shared their views and memories, and sometimes we went off-topic
In my opinion, the most interesting memory was from a woman who, during the pandemic
src="/media/Screenshot_۲۰۲۱۱۰۲۵-۲۳۱۰۲۷_Clubhouse-e1635247868829-151x300.jpg"Clubhouseکلاب هاوس
had to leave her previous job and start a home greenhouse business. She did this with minimal investment and also advised others to stop making excuses and start working. She said that you can start with any amount of money and suggested that greenhouse farming is very profitable.

In my opinion, change is easy for some people and difficult for others because they are in different conditions: mental, family, psychological, physical, environmental, and various other parameters

However, the biggest challenge for most people is the mental challenge that this decision-making entails
When thought is accompanied by strong positive feelings for change, a positive event occurs, and when it faces negative feelings, no change occurs
One of the biggest obstacles for people to change is laziness or procrastination
A person may know exactly that they need to change, but laziness doesn't allow them to
They see that their friends are progressing with changes in their lives, but still lack the courage and boldness to change, and this laziness is one of the biggest obstacles
Thinking about change alone is not enough, and having a plan and creating motivation and feeling of change is very effective
Another point is whether change is always necessary for us?
Perhaps you are working in a city or job, and influenced by advertisements and conversations of people, you leave your city. Here you have taken a risk and haven't thought well about this change, and it may bring you unexpected profit or loss.
There are many books about change, and many experts discuss this topic, and you can learn a lot with a simple search, but the important thing is to find your own formula for change
Because everyone must change in their own way and more importantly, implementing the change

Room Title:

Startup, Entrepreneurship, Team Building, and Commercialization of Ideas (Q&A)

In the initial part of our discussion, we talked about ideas and patents.
Some individuals who had registered patents believed that merely registering a patent is not sufficient and that commercialization is even more important than patent registration. A patent alone enhances the intellectual property aspect of the work, and some individuals, by modifying certain parts of
src="/media/Screenshot_۲۰۲۱۱۰۲۸-۱۹۰۵۳۹_Clubhouse-1-e1635455492736-271x300.jpg"Clubhouse Startup Room

The second part of the discussion focused on people's experiences in team building.
This team building, which often takes place before registering a company for a startup, is the most critical factor for individuals' success in advancing their projects.
If the human resources are not selected correctly and engineered, it will lead to deficiencies or the bankruptcy of the startup team.
Specialized individuals need to be managed in a way that they move together cohesively and unitedly toward the goal. Managing and strategizing human resources is a very important and vital task for the continuation of startups.
The third part of the discussion touched upon Q&A and how to develop and refine ideas.
We discussed how to work on ideas and presented several methods for implementing and validating ideas.
I also shared my personal opinion and the method I use for generating and nurturing ideas.

7286.content_en:
Greetings

A brief report on two rooms held in the Persian programmer Club – Clubhouse app

These days, I'm more present on Clubhouse and try to build connections and network through this platform. I also share my experiences with others and learn from their experiences and knowledge.
In Clubhouse, on Wednesday, November 3rd, during this beautiful autumn, we held two rooms. The first was about team building in startups, and the second was a friendly conversation among programmers and other professionals.

First, a brief report on the first room:

Topic » Brainstorming: How should startup team building be? Introduction, Collaboration
Duration » Approximately 33 minutes
I started the room at 9 PM in Clubhouse, and after a few minutes, friends joined us. We talked about the importance of team building in startups and heard from some of the people who were present.
The number of people in the room was usually between 5 to 15. Since I saw the attendance was a bit low, I decided to close the room to continue it at a more appropriate time with a different topic, as it's a very important discussion.

A brief report on the second room:

Topic » Friendly Conversation

Duration » Approximately 2 hours

I started a room around 11 PM in Clubhouse (in Persian Programmer Club), where mostly software experts, programmers, designers, and others were present. Unlike the first room, this one had more attendees.
It continued until about 1 AM and could have gone on longer, but since I had decided to go to bed earlier, we ended the room.
Many friends, mostly programmers, were present in the room and shared their thoughts. The discussions were more technical or about issues they were looking for solutions to. Fortunately, experts from all backgrounds were present and answered questions well.
At one point in the conversation, the discussion also turned to the migration of experts, with some in favor and a few against.
If I had to give a percentage, about 90% were in favor of experts migrating from Iran.
Someone introduced the UAE country and talked about its advantages for programmer immigration.
Startup discussions continued in this room, and we talked about some ideas and their applications in the software market.
I will try to hold more rooms with experts on other nights as well.
Thank you – Mehrdad

7928.content_en:
Continuing with the second through fifth phases of Iran's revolutionary corridor

🌐 Phase Two of the North-South Smart Corridor: Project Value from Four Key Perspectives

The text provides an extensive analysis of the second phase of the North-South Corridor project, outlining its significant geostrategic and economic value for Iran and the Eurasian region. The analysis estimates a substantial return on investment (ROI) of 28–32% on an estimated $8–$12 billion investment, projecting a swift payback period of under six years, primarily through transit fees and associated logistical services. Geopolitically, the source positions Iran as an “obligatory hub” due to its unique access to both the Caspian Sea and the Indian Ocean, offering a faster and more stable alternative to rival corridors involving Iraq, Turkey, or Pakistan. The document highlights Iran's competitive advantages, including existing infrastructure and proprietary Retrofit technology, which significantly reduces costs compared to competitors, ultimately promoting the corridor as a pathway for regional economic cooperation and non-oil revenue growth.

۱. Economic Perspective: Real Added Value

  • Estimated Investment: $8–$12 billion (for the first 1,200 km priority section)
  • Stable Annual Income (from year 6 onward): $2.4–$3.4 billion
  • Return on Investment (ROI):
    • Internal (IRR): ~28–32%
    • Payback Period: 4.5–5.5 years after operation begins
  • Cumulative Added Value (until 2040): $120–$180 billion
    • Includes direct (transit), indirect (industry, logistics), and induced employment effects

💡 Key Point: This project is not just a "railway" — it's an economic ecosystem where every dollar invested creates $3.2 in economic value (based on World Bank models for transit corridors).

۲. Geostrategic Perspective: Iran as an "Obligatory Hub"

  • Unique Position: The only country with access to both the Caspian Sea (connecting to Russia/Central Asia) and the Indian Ocean (Persian Gulf + Chabahar).
  • Reduced Dependence on the Strait of Hormuz: Chabahar + Bandar Abbas = a strategic solution for India and China during geopolitical crises.
  • Role in China's Initiative (BRI): Iran can replace Pakistan in the western part of the "Belt and Road" — especially given Pakistan's political instability.

🌍 Iran is not an option but a strategic necessity for many regional powers.

۳. Competitive Perspective: The Corridor Battlefront

While Iran works on the North-South Corridor, regional competitors are also active:
Iraq–Turkey–Europe Iraq, Turkey, European Union Proximity to Europe, Mediterranean ports Internal insecurity in Iraq, dependence on Turkey
China–Red–Jordan–Mediterranean China, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Israel Chinese capital, advanced technology Political tensions, high cost
Oman–Kuwait–Iraq (Southern Axis) Oman, Kuwait, Iraq Access to the Gulf, deep-water ports Lacks connection to Central Asia
Pakistan–Chabahar–Afghanistan (Chinese) China, Pakistan Chinese investment ($6 billion) Insecurity, corruption, dependence on China

✅ Iran's Competitive Advantage:

  • Bidirectional connection (North + South) — competitors only have one direction.
  • Existing rail infrastructure (12,000+ km of railways) — no need to build from scratch.
  • Domestic Retrofit technology — 80% cost reduction compared to competitors.
  • Strategic independence — no dependence on a single power (like China or the US).

🔥 Iran is the only country that can complete the "Complete Eurasia Corridor" in 14 days — without needing seas or risky political intermediaries.

۴. Investor Perspective: Why is this the golden opportunity now?

✅ Investment Incentives:

  • Intellectual Property Rights: Retrofit technology exportable to 15+ Central Asian and Caucasian countries.
  • Transit Free Zone: Proposal to create a special economic corridor zone with 10 years of tax exemption.
  • Government Guarantees: Cooperation with the National Development Fund and the Central Bank to guarantee return on investment.
  • Co-investment with Regional Powers: India (Chabahar), Russia (INSTC), UAE (logistics).

💰 Estimated Investment and Return:
Technology and R&D $200–300 million 3–4 years (through technology licensing)
Rail Infrastructure $6–8 billion 5–6 years (through tolls and services)
Logistics and Terminals $2–3 billion 4–5 years (through leasing and operations)

📈 Forecast: With a 12% growth in global transit in Eurasia (source: UNESCAP), this project could become Iran's largest non-oil cash flow by 2035.

🌱 Growth of Hope: Why cooperation on this project is a win for everyone?

  • For India: A secure and fast route to Europe without depending on Pakistan.
  • For Russia: Southern markets without sea sanctions.
  • For UAE and Oman: Access to Central Asia via Iran instead of Iraq.
  • For China: An alternative stable route in the west of BRI.
  • For Iran: Transformation from a "petroleum economy" to a "passage-technology economy".

🤝 This project is not a zero-sum game, but a multilateral collaboration where each partner becomes part of a victorious network.

✨ Final Summary of Phase Two: Not a Project, but a Historical Movement

Phase Two of the North-South Corridor is a strategic, economic, and historical opportunity:

  • Investment: 8–12 billion dollars
  • Return on Investment: 28–32% annually, return in less than 6 years
  • Competition: Iran leads with the advantage of "two-way connectivity + low-cost technology"
  • Hope: This corridor can be a bridge for economic peace in the region — where commercial interests soften political borders.

🚀 This is not just a railway. It is an invitation to collaborate in building a mirror of prosperity, connectivity, and progress for all Eurasian countries.

🚆 Phase Three: The East-West Intelligent Corridor of Iran and Connection to Neighbors

(Years 6 to 10 — Implementation Horizon: 2031–2035)

🎯 Strategic Objective

Creating the East-West Transit Axis of Iran as a complement to the North-South Corridor, with the aim of:

  • Connecting East Asia (China, India) to the Middle East and Europe (Turkey, Iraq, Jordan)
  • Transforming Iran into a two-dimensional transit hub of Eurasia (North-South + East-West)
  • Activating border economies and reducing regional inequality
  • Creating a integrated regional rail network within the framework of "civilizational cooperation, not zero-sum competition"

🌍 Why is Phase Three Essential?

After the success of Phase Two (North-South), Iran holds half of the Eurasian transit map. But without an East-West axis:

  • Incomplete transit capacity remains
  • Western neighboring countries (Iraq, Turkey) will turn to other competitors (like Saudi Arabia, Jordan)
  • China will only connect to Europe through Pakistan or Russia — not Iran

✨ Phase Three will transform Iran from a 'transit route' to the 'transit decision-making center of Eurasia'.

🗺️ Key Routes of Phase Three

1. Central East-West Axis (Priority One)

  • Route: Zahedan ← Kerman ← Yazd ← Isfahan ← Kermanshah → Khosravi Border (connection to Iraq)
  • Length: 1,400 kilometers
  • International Connections:
    • East: To Pakistan (Quetta) and China (via INSTC and BRI)
    • West: To Iraq (Baghdad), Turkey (Ankara), and from there to Europe

2. Northern East-West Axis (Priority Two)

  • Route: Mashhad ← Bojnourd ← Esfarayen ← Hamadan → Bazargan Border (connection to Turkey)
  • Length: 1,100 kilometers
  • Feature: Passing through underdeveloped regions of Northeast — creating developmental balance

3. Southern Axis (Connection to the Gulf and Oman)

  • Route: Bandar Abbas ← Kerman ← Zahedan → Mirjaveh Border (connection to Pakistan)
  • Integration with Chabahar: Connecting Chabahar to the East-West network to attract India-Europe transit

🔗 Smart Map: All these axes intersect with the North-South Corridor in Tehran, Isfahan, and Yazd — creating a star-shaped rail network (Hub-and-Spoke)

🌐 Key International Connections
China Zahedan ← Quetta ← Chabahar Cooperation within BRI + INSTC framework
India Chabahar ← Zahedan ← Isfahan Active transit agreement
Pakistan Mirjaveh–Quetta Technical negotiations in progress
Iraq Khosravi–Baghdad Initial agreement for rail connection
Turkey Bazargan–Ankara Cooperation within international railway framework
Afghanistan Doosti→Herat High potential (with future political stability)

💡 Iran is the only country that can directly connect China to Iraq and Turkey — without passing through Russia or the sea.

📊 Key Figures of Phase Three
Total length of new/rebuilt lines 2,500+ kilometers
Estimated Investment 14–18 billion dollars
Added Transit Capacity 50–70 million tons annually
Reduction in transit time (China–Europe) From 28 days to 16–18 days
Direct and Indirect Job Creation 200,000+ jobs
Stable annual income (from year 10) 3–4.5 billion dollars

🏗️ Key Technologies

Smart East-West Retrofit: Using the advanced technology from Phase One to rebuild old lines

  • Autonomous Freight Trains: Testing in low-traffic sections

Smart Energy Network: Integration of solar, wind, and storage at border stations

  • Integrated Digital Transit Platform: Ability to book, pay, and track cargo from China to Germany in one app

💰 Financial Model and Return on Investment

Financing Sources:

  • 40%: Chinese and Indian investment (within BRI and INSTC frameworks)
  • 30%: Regional development banks (like AIIB, EDB)
  • 20%: Iranian and international private sector (logistics, warehousing)
  • 10%: Government budget for strategic sectors

ROI and Return on Investment:

  • Return on Investment: 5–6 years after full operation
  • Internal Rate of Return (IRR): 25–30%
  • Non-financial returns: 30% reduction in carbon emissions in regional transportation

🌱 Values Beyond Economics

  • Development of underprivileged regions: 70% of the route passes through disadvantaged provinces (Sistan, Khorasan, Kurdistan)
  • Economic peace: Creating interdependence with neighbors — replacing "co-growth economy" with "zero-sum competition"
  • Energy independence: Use of renewable energy at 60% of stations
  • Software power: Iran recognized as the architect of the Eurasia transit network

📅 Implementation Timeline
Year 6 – Technical-international studies
– Attracting initial capital ($3-4 billion)
– Signing agreements with Iraq and Pakistan
Years 7-8 – Starting construction of priority sections (Zahedan-Isfahan, Isfahan-Khosravi)
– Launching the digital transit platform
Year 9 – Testing transit trains from China to Iraq
– Opening the first smart border terminals
Year 10 – Full operation of the central axis
– Complete connection to the railway networks of Turkey and Pakistan

✨ Phase 3 Summary: Iran, the Beating Heart of the Eurasian Network

Phase 3 is the crowning achievement of Iran's strategic rail project. With its completion:

  • Iran will be the only country that connects all four geographical directions (north, south, east, west).
  • The cumulative value of the project (Phases 1-3) will reach $300+ billion by 2040.
  • 400,000+ jobs will be created — mostly in regions where young people are emigrating today.

 

🚆 Phase 4: Iran's Comprehensive Rail Network — From Global Corridors to Local Streets

(Years 11-20 — Implementation Horizon: 2036-2045)

🎯 Strategic Objective

  • Connect all cities with populations over 50,000 to the national railway network
  • Expand Iran's rail network from the current ~12,000 km to 35,000-40,000 km
  • Transform rail into the backbone of domestic transportation (target: 40% share in passenger and 30% in freight transport by 2045)
  • Reduce dependence on cars and roads → reducing traffic, pollution, and accidents

💡 This phase transforms rail from "an international transit medium" to "the daily means of transportation for every Iranian."

🗺️ Network Vision: Three Intelligent Layers

1. Layer 1: International and National High-Speed Corridors (developed in Phases 2 and 3)

  • Speed: 160-250 km/h
  • Routes: Tehran-Mashhad, Tehran-Shiraz, Tehran-Tabriz, Tehran-Ahvaz, and border connections

2. Layer 2: Regional Rail Lines

  • Connect all provincial centers and cities with 100,000+ population
  • Speed: 100-160 km/h
  • Train frequency: Every 2-4 hours
  • Examples: Ardabil-Zanjan, Yasuj-Shiraz, Gorgan-Sari

3. Layer 3: Urban and Suburban Rail

  • Connect cities with 50,000-100,000 population to provincial centers or large cities
  • Speed: 60-100 km/h
  • System type: Light Rail or advanced trams
  • Examples:
    • Savadieh ← Tehran
    • Nishapur ← Mashhad
    • Dezful ← Ahvaz

7975.content_en:
BIZPAL Digital Sales, Marketing and Advertising Startup

The BIZPAL startup was formed with the goal of revolutionizing the world of digital sales, marketing, and advertising; a place where data, artificial intelligence, and creativity work hand in hand to create real, measurable growth for businesses. In today's competitive era, brands no longer just need tools for advertising, but they need a smart business partner that can think, analyze, and automatically execute the best decisions.

 

The provided text is an excerpt from a comprehensive pitch deck written in Farsi for potential investors in an AI-driven business assistant named BizPal. This document outlines a solution to the problem of disorganized sales and marketing among small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) in Iran, where ninety percent lack professional teams. BizPal is presented as an AI commercial assistant that forecasts sales, runs high-ROI advertising campaigns, and automates personalized marketing using a subscription-based Software as a Service (SaaS) model. The pitch details the target market of 2.5 million SMEs, current progress including a successful MVP test demonstrating a 37% increase in sales, and a request for $300,000 in Pre-Seed funding to achieve a goal of 10,000 paying users within eighteen months. The central competitive distinction is that BizPal thinks, acts, and learns, differentiating it from traditional CRM and generic chatbot tools.

BIZPAL Startup Introduction

In a world where the speed of trend changes exceeds the speed of managerial decision-making, BIZPAL has entered the arena as a smart sales and business assistant to shorten and make the path of company growth more efficient by analyzing data and automatically executing advertising, marketing, and sales campaigns.

BIZPAL's goal is to provide a platform that, in addition to managing advertising and customer communication, serves as a 24/7 personal assistant for business managers; a companion that understands what the market wants, how the customer feels, and what the brand should say to sell.​

Plan Summary and Key Features

  1. Smart Sales Assistant (AI Sales Assistant): Predict potential customers, automatically generate invoices, and alert for customer churn.

  2. Automated Advertising and Marketing Intelligence: Design and optimize campaigns based on real data, generate advertising content, and allocate budget to high-performance channels.

  3. Customer Management and Communication (Smart CRM): Personalize customer communications and analyze behavioral data for customer retention.

  4. Management Dashboard and Data Analytics (BI Dashboard): Real-time display of advertising, sales performance and ROI with automatic suggestions.

  5. Sales-focused Chatbot: Direct interaction with users, identifying needs, and completing the purchase process in-chat.

The platform's revenue model is designed based on monthly subscription (SaaS) and with an initial development cost of approximately 120 to 170 thousand US dollars, it has the potential for return on investment in less than one year.​

Conclusion

BIZPAL is not just a software; it's a smart sales and marketing partner that helps businesses see the future before it happens and make more accurate, faster, and more profitable decisions.
In a world where competition becomes tighter every day, BIZPAL has come to place intelligence, speed, and creativity at the service of real brand growth.

8014.content_en:
Introduction: Iran's Strategic Role in the Regional Economic Geography

In a world that is rapidly reshaping business and logistics patterns, Iran's geographical position as a natural bridge between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East has always been presented as a strategic opportunity for economic development. However, the images presented depict a concerning reality: Iran is being removed from emerging trade corridors. this removal is not due to internal incapability, but rather the result of China and Russia's active alignment with Israel and America in creating and developing alternative routes that bypass Iran. This article comprehensively examines this phenomenon, its causes, key related projects, and its implications for Iran's national security and economy.

Why is Iran's removal from trade corridors happening due to the alignment of China and Russia with Israel and America and...?

The good news is that we have a solution!

Get the solution at the end of the article

Part One: A Chart of Strategic Elimination – Analysis of the "Geoeconomic Isolation of Iran" Chart

The chart presented in the first image, titled "Geoeconomic Isolation of Iran in Emerging Trade Corridors," provides a powerful visual representation of Iran's current situation. This "network map" type chart shows key cities and trade corridors, marking Iran with a star. Notably, none of the major corridor lines pass through Iran. In contrast, numerous routes include:

 

  • IMEC (India-Middle East-Europe Corridor): Passing through ports in India (Mumbai), the Persian Gulf (Dubai, Jebel Ali), and Israel (Haifa, Piraeus).
  • CPEC (China-Pakistan Economic Corridor): Starting from Gwadar, Pakistan, and connecting to Karachi and Kashmir.
  • Zangezur Corridor: Passing through southeastern Armenia and western Azerbaijan.
  • Middle Corridor: Passing through the Caucasus and Central Asia (Baku, Tbilisi, Tashkent).

This chart clearly shows that Iran is an isolated point within these new networks. This "geoeconomic isolation" is not a coincidence, but the result of a policy strategy in which China and Russia, in cooperation with Israel and America, have designed routes that bypass and exclude Iran from the regional economic flow.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-r57-238x300.png"

Part Two: Key Projects that Exclude Iran

Next, we examine the strategic projects that have directly or indirectly led to Iran's exclusion from trade corridors.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-77-ب-238x300.png"

1. India-Middle East-Europe Corridor (IMEC)

This corridor, introduced at the September 2023 G20 summit as an India-Israel-Saudi-Europe corridor, aims to create a completely alternative route to Iran's North-South Corridor. This route, passing through European Mediterranean ports (Piraeus) and Israeli ports (Haifa), and Indian ports (Mumbai), bypasses Iran and is implemented with the cooperation of countries such as Israel, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, India, Italy, the USA, and the European Union. This corridor is not just a trade route, but a political tool for creating a new "economic axis" that excludes Iran.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-5-218x300.png"

2. Saudi Arabia-China-Gulf Cooperation Agreement

In China's heavy investment in new ports in Jizan, Sudan, and Djibouti, the goal is to transfer energy from the Persian Gulf to East Africa and the Mediterranean without needing Iran. These projects, known as the "Red Sea and East Africa," have been sidelined from the Chinese port chain due to sanctions and regional tensions. This action has dealt a direct blow to Iran's strategic position in controlling the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman.

3. The "Turkey-Azerbaijan-Nakhchivan" Project (Zangezur Corridor)

This project, which has been operationally implemented, provides a completely alternative route for Azerbaijan to connect with the Nakhchivan Republic (which is landlocked by Iran). This corridor, implemented through Armenia with the support of Turkey and Azerbaijan, bypasses Iran, meaning Iran's exclusion from this transit route. This project also serves as a political tool to weaken Iran in the Caucasus region.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-ل-200x300.png"

4. Expansion of Russia's Transit Routes through Central Asia

Russia, by creating new transit routes through Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan and the Caspian Sea to India and China, has removed Iran from its transit routes. These routes, created due to banking and insurance sanctions against Iran, do not pass through Iran's Bandar Abbas and Gwadar ports, instead using Russian and Kazakh ports.

5. The Role of the UAE, Qatar, and Oman in Maritime Transit

The Arab countries of the southern Persian Gulf, with heavy investment in Jebel Ali and Hamad ports, are seeking to create a new logistics hub that bypasses Iran. By supporting alternative routes and competing with Iranian ports, these countries play a key role in excluding Iran from trade corridors.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-4-240x300.png"

6. China's Strategic Shift (Reducing Dependence on the Iranian Route)

China, predicting that Iran will not be able to play a key role in transit routes for the next few years, has moved towards alternative routes like CPEC and BRI. This strategic shift, made considering regional security and economic developments, has led to a reduction in China's dependence on Iran and an increased dependence on Pakistan and Kazakhstan.

src="/media/mehrdad-startup-1-33-195x300.png"

7. The Collapse of Iran's Role in the Regional Energy and Fuel Supply Market

Despite its rich oil and gas reserves, Iran has been sidelined from its key role in the regional energy market due to oil sanctions and an inability to supply regional fuel. This situation, resulting from international sanctions and Iran's inability to provide logistics and transit services, has diminished Iran's importance in the regional oil and gas markets.

8. Internal Crisis and Banking and Insurance Sanctions

No global trade route is willing to pass through a country under banking, insurance, and SWIFT sanctions. This internal crisis, stemming from international sanctions and Iran's inability to provide logistics and transit services, has led to Iran's exclusion from global trade corridors.

9. Increased Israeli Presence in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea

Israel, with Emirati and Bahraini cooperation, is establishing a direct presence in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. This presence, carried out with the support of the US and the EU, has created a "blind spot" area around Iran. This area, extending from the coastline, means Iran's exclusion from regional trade corridors.

10. Changes in Global Insurance and Shipping Routes after the Gaza War

Large insurance and shipping companies, due to insecurity in the Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb regions, have chosen alternative routes through East Africa and the Mediterranean. This route change, which is due to regional tensions and increased insurance costs, has led to a decrease in shipping volume in Iran.

Part Three: Iran's Military and Strategic Response

In the fourth image, a photo of Commander of the Army Navy, Shahram Noveisi, is presented. In this image, he at a conference, with reference to his speech, said that unprecedentedly few military officials had clarified to this extent: "The entire effort and strategy of the enemy is to limit the corridors so that only they can benefit from them and somehow eliminate us." This statement is an explicit admission by Iranian military officials of the reality of Iran's elimination from trade corridors.

He continues: "In the same speech, he warned that Iran's development documents should be written based on strategic regenerative foundations, while developments are oblivious to the changes in new regional realities. His emphasis was that if our perspective remains from 'shore to sea' and not vice versa, Iran will gradually be erased from the role of global trade."

This statement shows that Iranian military officials have realized the reality of Iran's elimination from trade corridors and are formulating new strategies to deal with this situation. However, these strategies, which are based on Iranian "geopolitical changes," have not yet been implemented operationally and require a profound change in Iran's economic and security policymaking.

Part Four: Conclusion and Iran's Future in Trade Corridors

Finally, the fifth image provides a key summary of Iran's situation in trade corridors. This summary, which begins with "If we want to summarize," shows that Iran has been mapped out for elimination in the 1400s. This elimination has occurred in four main axes:

  1. East (Turkey-Europe): By creating the Zangezur corridor.
  2. West (Turkey-Europe): By creating the IMEC corridor.
  3. North (Caucasus): By creating the CPEC corridor.
  4. South (China-Pakistan): By creating the CPEC corridor.

This elimination is not a coincidence, but the result of a policy strategy in which China and Russia, with the cooperation of Israel and America, have designed routes that bypass Iran and exclude it from the regional economic flow. This situation has not only been an economic blow but also a strategic blow to Iran's national security.

Finally, this article concludes that Iran, to prevent complete elimination from trade corridors, needs a profound change in economic and security policymaking. This change must include internal reforms, reduction of sanctions, creation of regional cooperation, and strengthening of Iran's strategic position in the region. Otherwise, Iran will remain in the coming decades as a landlocked and economically isolated country.
